conversation.content: Let's design a URL shortening service — like bit.ly or TinyURL. Users submit a long URL and get back a short one that redirects. What questions do you have?
How many URLs will people create per day? And how long do the short URLs last — forever?
100 million new URLs per day, with a 100:1 read-to-write ratio. URLs expire after 5 years by default. Any other questions?
Can users choose their own custom short URL? Like bit.ly/my-product-launch?
Yes, custom aliases should be supported. Let's start designing. What are the main API endpoints?

Two endpoints. POST /shorten takes a long URL and optionally a custom alias, returns the short URL. GET /{short_code} redirects the user to the long URL. Maybe also a DELETE to remove a URL and a GET /stats/{short_code} for analytics.
Good. How would you generate the short code? If someone submits 'https://example.com/very/long/path', how do we produce 'abc123'?

I'd hash the URL. Like, take the MD5 hash of the long URL and use the first 7 characters. That would give us a short code. MD5 always gives the same hash for the same input, so the same long URL would always get the same short code.
What happens if two different long URLs produce the same first 7 characters of their MD5 hash? With 100 million URLs per day, collisions become very likely.

Oh right, collisions. When we generate the short code, we'd check if it already exists in the database. If it does, we could... append something? Like add a character or rehash with a salt until we get a unique one. But that could be slow if there are many collisions.

Rehashing can work but is inefficient. Another approach: instead of hashing the URL, generate a unique ID first and then convert it to a short code. If the ID is unique, the code is unique — no collisions. How might you generate unique IDs?

An auto-incrementing counter? Each new URL gets the next number — 1, 2, 3... Then convert the number to base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) to make it shorter. Number 1000000 in base62 is only a few characters. No collisions because each number is unique.
Right — base62 encoding of a unique counter is a clean approach. But with multiple servers handling requests, how do you ensure the counter doesn't produce duplicates?

Hmm, if two servers both try to increment at the same time... they might get the same number. We could use a single database auto-increment column, but that becomes a bottleneck. Or maybe each server gets its own range? Like server 1 gets IDs 1-10000, server 2 gets 10001-20000, and so on. When a server uses up its range, it requests a new batch.
Range-based allocation is a good solution. Now, where do you store the URL mappings? What database?

The data is simple — just short_code → long_url. It's basically a key-value lookup. I could use a relational database like MySQL, but a key-value store might be more efficient since we mostly do point lookups. Maybe DynamoDB? It scales well for simple key-value access patterns and handles the write throughput.
DynamoDB or a relational database are both valid. With 100:1 read-write ratio, reads dominate. How would you make reads faster?

A cache in front of the database. Redis. When someone clicks a short URL, check Redis first. If it's there, redirect immediately. If not, check the database, put the result in Redis, then redirect. Popular URLs will be served entirely from cache. With the 80/20 rule, 20% of URLs probably get 80% of traffic, so the cache would have a high hit rate.
Good. When a user clicks the short URL, should the server return a 301 or 302 redirect? What's the difference?

301 is permanent redirect — the browser caches it. 302 is temporary. I think 301 is better because it's cached so subsequent visits don't hit our servers at all? But wait, if we cache in the browser, we can't track clicks for analytics. So maybe 302 if we want analytics, 301 if we just want fast redirects.
Good trade-off. We're almost out of time. Any final thoughts?

Rate limiting on the creation endpoint so people don't abuse it. And a cleanup job that runs periodically to delete expired URLs — the ones past their 5-year TTL. And for custom aliases, we'd need to validate they're not taken and don't contain inappropriate words.
Good practical additions. Thanks for the discussion — you covered the core components well.

strengths: Arrived at range-based ID allocation independently when guided toward the problem
Good 301 vs 302 trade-off analysis — connected redirect choice to analytics requirements
Reasonable database choice with DynamoDB and solid caching strategy
weaknesses: No capacity estimation — didn't calculate storage needs, QPS, or cache sizing
Initial encoding approach (MD5 truncation) showed limited preparation — this is a well-known URL shortener design question
No failure handling — didn't discuss what happens if the database or cache goes down
Didn't discuss geographic distribution or CDN for the redirect endpoint
